title: Don't spoil it with reminders
hook: a kind word is better than charity followed by hurt (2:263–264)

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven ears of grain, and your line, one grain, seven hundred. Did you give the small thing? Today, al-Baqarah tells you how a gift can be lost after it's given. Day three hundred sixty.

Every family has one. The relative who helped you move, years ago, and has mentioned it at every holiday since. Remember when I drove the truck? Remember who paid for the pizza? The help was real. But somewhere around the tenth reminder, you start to wish they hadn't helped at all. The gift has turned into a debt you can never finish paying. Al-Baqarah knows this relative. Today: don't spoil it with reminders.
screen: `THE RELATIVE WHO HELPED YOU MOVE.` → `REMEMBER WHEN I DROVE THE TRUCK?` → `A GIFT TURNED INTO A DEBT.`

segments.voice: Right after the seven ears of grain, the surah adds a condition. Verse two hundred sixty-two: those who spend and then don't follow it with reminders of their generosity, or with hurt, their reward is with their Lord. Verse two hundred sixty-three, in Pickthall's words: “A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury.” The Arabic for those reminders is mann: bringing up the favor, holding it over someone. Then verse two sixty-four gives the picture of what mann does. A smooth rock with a thin layer of soil on it. It looks like a field. Then heavy rain falls, and washes it bare. Nothing grows. That's a gift spoiled by reminders: it looked like soil, but there was only stone underneath. The very next verse paints the opposite. A garden on high ground. Heavy rain falls, and it doubles its fruit. And if no heavy rain comes, even a light drizzle is enough. That's the gift given for God's sake, with no strings: it grows whatever weather comes. The tradition takes mann seriously. A hadith in Sahih Muslim names three people God will not speak to on the Day of Judgment, and one of them is al-mannan, the one who reminds people of what he gave. Notice what the verse ranks above a spoiled gift: a kind word. You can give nothing at all, and say something gentle, and that's better than money with a sting. Give and forget.
screen: `NO REMINDERS, NO HURT` · `A KIND WORD IS BETTER` · `THE ROCK WASHED BARE` · `THE GARDEN ON THE HILL`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give without mentioning it later. Sit, and think of something good you've done for someone that you've brought up since, out loud or in your head. The favor you keep score of. Picture it like a stone you've been carrying. Now picture setting it down by the road and walking on, without looking back. If you pray, you can leave it with God. If you don't, simply let it go. The bell holds the time.
Don't spoil it with reminders. Al-Baqarah's warning: reminders and hurt wash a gift away like rain off a rock; a kind word is better than a gift with a sting. Today's word.
screen: `DON'T SPOIL IT WITH REMINDERS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: give and forget. Today, do one kind thing, and don't mention it to anyone, including the person you did it for. Day three hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Muslims are taught to give without reminding the recipient or expecting thanks; mann, recounting one's favors, is counted a serious fault, and many give quietly so as not to be tempted toward it.

fork.setup: you helped a friend through a hard month. now you're annoyed with them. what does al-Baqarah say about bringing it up?
fork.reveal: don't follow a gift with reminders or hurt: it washes away like soil from a rock. a kind word is better.

original.note: Arabic: reminding someone of a favor, holding it over them; one who does it is al-mannan.

trapdoor: what you thought: be humble about giving.
what it means: reminders and hurt can undo a gift, the way rain strips a thin layer of soil off a rock.
what a scholar hears: the paired parables of 2:264–265, rock and hillside garden, and the hadith in Muslim naming al-mannan among three God will not speak to.
